examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Odd Functions
examples.problem: Given that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1} x\cos x \, \textrm dx = A,$ what is the value of $\displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 x\cos x  \, \textrm dx?$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Notice that $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) =  x\cos x$ is an odd function, we have

$$
\int_{-1}^{1} x\cos x  \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+A & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt[3]{x}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-2}^{4}\frac{7{x}^{3}}{1+2{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\sqrt[3]{-x} \\  & =-\sqrt[3]{x} \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt[3]{x}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(-x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & \ne -g(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $h(x)=\frac{7{x}^{3}}{1+2{x}^{4}}$ is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}h(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
